reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Trachyonychia produces rough, brittle, longitudinally ridged nails with a sandpaper-like surface, often with a loss of lustre
It may affect several or all twenty nails, hence the older term twenty-nail dystrophy, and is more common in children
It is a reaction pattern of the nail matrix rather than a single disease, and is associated with alopecia areata, lichen planus, and psoriasis
Two clinical forms are recognised: an opaque, rough sandpaper type and a shinier variety with numerous small superficial pits
It is usually a benign, cosmetic problem that does not scar the nail, particularly in the idiopathic childhood form
Diagnosis is generally clinical, and matrix biopsy is reserved for atypical cases because the appearance rarely predicts the underlying association
Management is largely supportive with reassurance and nail protection, as many childhood cases improve spontaneously over years
reference.pathophysiology: Trachyonychia reflects inflammation of the nail matrix that disturbs the orderly production of the nail plate, so that the emerging nail is irregular, rough, and ridged. The matrix inflammation is a shared final pathway for several conditions, including alopecia areata, lichen planus, psoriasis, and eczema, which is why the clinical appearance alone seldom identifies the cause. Because the inflammation usually affects the matrix without destroying it, the process is generally non-scarring and the nail can recover, although the widespread involvement of many nails reflects a diffuse matrix response.
additionalDifferentials: Nail lichen planus (with risk of scarring and pterygium in severe cases)
Chronic eczema affecting the nail matrix
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of all twenty nails and the hair and skin for associated disease
Onychoscopy to characterise pitting, ridging, and surface changes
Assessment for alopecia areata, lichen planus, and psoriasis elsewhere
Nail matrix biopsy reserved for atypical, scarring, or diagnostically uncertain cases
Mycology if fungal infection needs to be excluded
Longitudinal review to monitor spontaneous improvement, especially in children
redFlags: Features suggesting nail lichen planus with scarring, such as pterygium formation, which needs prompt attention
Rapidly progressive or destructive nail change inconsistent with benign trachyonychia
Associated systemic or extensive cutaneous disease requiring specific treatment
Single-nail atypical change that does not fit the diffuse pattern and warrants biopsy
reference.prognosis: Trachyonychia is generally benign and non-scarring, and the idiopathic childhood form often resolves spontaneously over several years, although nails associated with lichen planus can occasionally scar and warrant closer follow-up.
pitfalls: Over-investigating a benign, self-limiting childhood presentation
Missing scarring lichen planus of the nail, which requires earlier intervention
Assuming a fungal cause and treating with antifungals without confirmation
Promising rapid resolution when recovery is typically slow over months to years
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Reassure and observe, particularly in the idiopathic childhood form, which is benign, non-scarring and usually resolves spontaneously over several years
General nail care with emollients and hydration, nail-hardening lacquers, and avoidance of trauma and irritants to limit brittleness
Treat any associated matrix dermatosis, using topical or intralesional corticosteroids for lichen planus and vitamin D analogues or corticosteroids for psoriasis
Intralesional corticosteroid injection to the nail matrix for troublesome or refractory disease
Screen for and manage coexisting alopecia areata, lichen planus and psoriasis elsewhere on the skin and hair
Reserve nail matrix biopsy for atypical or scarring cases, with closer follow-up where lichen planus threatens permanent nail damage
